Symmetric Strategies

← Back to Index

1 Symmetric Strategies

If there is no restriction on the memory-number and the replica number, we can lower-bound the strategy through the symmetric of the property. We first define general testing strategy rigorously.

NoteDefinition

A property \mathcal{P} \subset \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}) is a set of quantum states. A two-outcome POVM \{E,\mathbb{I} - E\} on k-copies of n-qubit states tests the property \mathcal{P} iff for certain 1>\varepsilon_B \geq \varepsilon_A >0 and \delta = \Theta(1), \begin{align} d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P}) \leq \varepsilon_A \Rightarrow \text{tr}(E \rho^{\otimes k}) \geq 1/2 +\delta,\\ d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P}) \geq \varepsilon_B \Rightarrow \text{tr}(E \rho^{\otimes k}) \leq 1/2 - \delta. \end{align}

Now suppose the testing property \mathcal{P}, which is a set of state within n-qubit space, is invariant under unitary operation U(G) , which is a subgroup of U(2)^{\otimes n}. Namely, \begin{align} \forall \sigma \in \mathcal{P},\forall V \in U(G), V\sigma V^\dagger \in \mathcal{P}. \end{align} Then we are prepared to show that it is enough to consider the symmetric version of the strategy rather than an arbitrary POVM within n-qubit space, as stated by Lemma below

ImportantLemma

Given a k-replica strategy \{E, \mathbb{I } - E\} for the U(G)-symmetric property \mathcal{P} on n-qubits, the symmetric strategy \{\Phi(E), \mathbb{I } - \Phi(E)\} with \Phi(E) := |U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)} V^{\dagger,\otimes k}EV^{\otimes k} and \Phi_k(E) := |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \text{SWAP}_\pi E\cdot\text{SWAP}_\pi has non-decreasing efficiency.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. Because the unitary invariant property of \mathcal{P} and the non-decreasing property of trace distance under unitary transformation d_{\text{tr}}(\cdot,\cdot) = d_{\text{tr}}(U\cdot U^\dagger,U\cdot U^\dagger), we conclude that \begin{align} d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P}) \leq \varepsilon_A &\Rightarrow \forall U \in U(G), d_{\text{tr}}(U\rho U^\dagger, \mathcal{P}) \leq \varepsilon_A \\ &\Rightarrow \forall U \in U(G),\text{tr}( EU^{\otimes k}\rho^{\otimes k} U^{\dagger,\otimes k}) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1),\\ &\Leftrightarrow \forall U \in U(G),|U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)}\text{tr}(U^{\dagger,\otimes k} EU^{\otimes k}\rho^{\otimes k} ) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1),\\ &\Leftrightarrow \forall U \in U(G),\text{tr}(\bar E\rho^{\otimes k} ) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1) \end{align} Similarly, we can prove that d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P}) \geq \varepsilon_B \Rightarrow \text{tr}(\bar E \rho^{\otimes k}) \leq 1/2 - \Theta(1). The same procedure is applied for \bar{E} := |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \text{SWAP}_\pi E\cdot\text{SWAP}_\pi. Thus, we prove that the symmetric strategy \{\bar{E}, \mathbb{I } - \bar{E}\} will have at least the same testing efficiency. ◻

Then we discuss the symmetry for the estimation problem.

NoteDefinition

A quantitative property of states is a map f: \rho \to \mathbb{R} with \rho \in \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}) . Given a POVM \{M_m\}_{m \in R} on k-replica space, an k-replica estimator of f is an observable O \in \text{End}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}) such that \text{tr}(O \rho^{\otimes k}) = f(\rho). An estimator O is efficient k-replica strategy iff \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O)\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O') for all O \in \text{End}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}).

We say a quantitative property f is invariant under unitary operation U(G) iff f(U\cdot U^\dagger) = f(\cdot), \forall U \in U(G). The we gives the symmetric strategy for estimate problem.

ImportantLemma

If O is a k-replica estimator for property f. Then the symmetrized estimators \begin{align} \Phi(O):= |U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)} V^{\dagger,\otimes k}OV^{\otimes k},\Phi_{k}(O):= |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \mathbb{P}_\pi^{d,\dagger} \cdot O\cdot \mathbb{P}_\pi^{d}, \end{align} always satisfied \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(\Phi(O))\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O),\text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(\Phi_k(O))\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O).

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. We will show a more general statement for arbitrary channel that is unital (\Phi(\mathbb{I}) = \mathbb{I}), positive (\forall \rho \succeq 0, \Phi(\rho) \succeq 0), and satisfied \forall O \in \text{Herm}(\mathcal{H}), \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)) = \text{tr}(\rho O). By definition, \text{Var}_{\rho}(\Phi(O)) = \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2) - \text{tr}^2(\rho \Phi(O)) = [\text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2) - \text{tr}(\rho O^2)]+ \text{Var}_{\rho}(O). According to Theorem, \Phi(O^2)-\Phi(O)^2\succeq 0, which shows that \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2)<\text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O^2)) = \text{tr}(\rho O^2). This directly gives the result \text{Var}_{\rho}(\Phi(O)) \leq \text{Var}_{\rho}(O). ◻

Thanks to the Lemma and Lemma , if we find the lower bound of the sample complexity of all the symmetric POVM and operators, any strategy’s sample complexity is lower bounded by this value.

1.1 The unitary case U(G) = U(2^n)

The simplest case are properties that is invariant under a unitary transformation. The lemma is useful because any spectrum testing strategy \{M,\mathbb{I} - M\} now can be restated as weak Schur sampling followed by classical post-processing  [1], as stated by the theorem below.

ImportantLemma

Given a testing strategy \{M, \mathbb{I } - M\} for unitary invariant property \mathcal{P} such that: \begin{align} \tr(M \rho^{\otimes k}) &\geq 1 - \delta,\forall \rho \in \mathcal{P};\\ \tr(M \rho^{\otimes k}) &\leq 1 - f(\varepsilon),\forall \rho ~\varepsilon \text{-far from~} \mathcal{P}. \end{align} Another strategy \bar{M} such that [\bar M,U^{\otimes k}] =0 and [\bar M,\text{SWAP}_\pi]=0 can be constructed with non-decreasing efficiency.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. M_s =|S_k|^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in S^k}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n}\cdot M \cdot\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n} have unchanged efficiency because \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n}\cdot \rho^{\otimes k} \cdot\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n} = \rho^{\otimes k}. Combined with lemma proves the result. ◻

This construction simplified the analysis because we can reduce arbitrary strategy to a canonical one-weak Shur sampling. To see this, we first cite the lemma in  [2], according to the famous Schur-Weyl duality.

ImportantLemma

Given the symmetry group S_k , use \kappa \vdash k labels the conjugate classes K(\kappa) and \lambda \vdash k label the irreducible representation with the character function \chi_{\lambda}(\cdot) and dimension \text{dim}~\lambda. Define the projective measurements P_\lambda and the conjugate-class observables O_{\kappa} as \begin{align} P_{\lambda} := (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \mathbb{P}_\pi^d,\quad O_{\kappa} := |K(\kappa)|^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in K(\kappa)} \mathbb{P}_\pi^d. \end{align} If \forall U \in \mathbb{C}^{k} and \forall \pi \in S_k, the operator M on the space (\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes k} satisfies [M,U^{\otimes k}] =0 and [M,\mathbb{P}_\pi^d]=0, then M can be decomposed as \begin{align} M &= \sum_{\lambda \vdash k} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda,\quad M = \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} O_\kappa, \label{eq:M_decomp} \\ &\text{where~}O_{\kappa} = \sum_{\lambda}{(\text{dim}\lambda)^{-1}}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa) P_{\lambda}. \label{eq:relation_PM} \end{align}

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. The proof of this theorem is separated into three steps. First, by Schur-Weyl duality, we know that [M,U^{\otimes k}]=0 iff M is a linear superposition of SWAP gates: \begin{align} \label{eq:M_decomp_mid} M &= \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot \text{SWAP}_g. \end{align}

Then we show that linear combination of SWAP gates commute with all the SWAP gates iff the superposition coefficient is a class function. According to Eq.~(eq:M_decomp_mid), M is the image of group algebra m = \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) g under representation \rho(g) = \text{SWAP}_g. Then m must commute with arbitray element in S_k. \forall~ h \in S_k, notice that: \begin{align} hmh^{-1} &= \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot{hgh^{-1}} =\sum_{t \in S_k} f(h^{-1} t h) \cdot{t} =\sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot g = m \end{align} This then imply f(g) = f(h^{-1} t h) for all h \in S_k and f is a class function. Last, given that character functions forms a orthonormal basis for class function, we obtain f(g) = \sum_{\lambda}c_{\lambda} \chi_{\lambda}(g). Plug into Eq.~(eq:M_decomp_mid) gives: \begin{align} M &= \sum_{\lambda}c_{\lambda} \sum_{g \in S_k}\chi_{\lambda}(g)\cdot \text{SWAP}_g =\sum_{\lambda} \alpha_{\lambda} \frac{\text{dim}(V_\lambda)}{k!} \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \text{SWAP}_\pi = \sum_{\lambda} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda \end{align} This is indeed a projector based on Lemma proved before. To prove the conclusion (ii), we first noted that \begin{align} \sum_{\lambda}\frac{1}{\text{dim~}\lambda}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa) P_{\lambda} &= \sum_{\pi \in S_k} ({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\lambda}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa) \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \mathbb{P}^d_\pi\\ &=|K(\kappa)|^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in K(\kappa)} \mathbb{P}^d_\pi = O_{\kappa} \end{align} Here in the second line we use the second orthogonal identity |G|^{-1}\sum_{p}\chi_{p}(\kappa_j)\chi_{p}(\kappa_k) = |K(\kappa_k)|^{-1}\delta_{jk}. Then plug in Eq.~(eq:M_decomp) we get \begin{align} \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} O_\kappa =\sum_{\lambda\vdash k}\frac{1}{\text{dim}~\lambda}\left[ \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} \chi_{\lambda}(\kappa)\right] P_{\lambda}= \sum_{\lambda \vdash k} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda. \end{align} This implys the transformation (\text{dim}\lambda)\cdot \alpha_{\lambda} = \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} \chi_{\lambda}(\kappa). ◻

1.2 Examples.

When k = 2, the group S_2 only has two conjugate class (2,0) and (1,1). The corresponding projectors are P_{(2,0)} = 2^{-1}{(\mathbb{I} + \text{SWAP}_{(1,2)})},P_{(1,1)} = 2^{-1}{(\mathbb{I} - \text{SWAP}_{(1,2)})}. This is just the SWAP test of two identical states, which is widely used for purity test. For larger t, the computation of those exact projector is proved to be #P-hard  [3]. Fortunately, the realization of projective measurement \{P_\lambda\} can be implemented in time \text{Poly}(k,\ln d) with generalized phase estimation circuit  [4], which is efficient for n-qubits property testing with d = 2^n. This is called the weak Schur sampling (WSS). Now we characterize the result of WSS by polynomials of density matrix’s spectrum.

NoteDefinition

Let \mu,\lambda\vdash k be a partition of the replica number k. Let \mathcal{T} be the set of all semi-standard Young tableaus with shape \lambda and alphabet \{1,\cdots,d\}. Let \#(T,i) be the number of times that the character i occurs in the semi-standard Young tableau T. Two rank-k symmetric polynomials of d variables \mathbf{x}=(x_1,\cdots,x_d) can be defined below.

  • Schur polynomial (SP) is a rank-k symmetric polynomial that s_{\lambda}(\mathbf x):= \sum_{T}\prod_{i=1}^d x_i^{\#(T,i)}

  • Power sum polynomial (PSP) is a rank-k symmetric polynomial that M_{\mu}(\mathbf{x}):=\prod_{i=1}^{l(\mu)} \sum_{j=1}^d x_j^{\mu_i}

1.3 Examples.

If we take \lambda = (k,0,\cdots), we get the \sum_{j = 1}^d x_j^k. SP and PSP can decompose each other, as shown in Lemma below.

ImportantLemma

Any rank-k power sum polynomial can be decomposed with the rank-k symmetric Schur polynomial through M_{\mu}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\lambda \vdash k}\chi_{\lambda}(\mu)s_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}).

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

Refer to  [5], the distribution of \text{tr}(P_{\lambda} \rho^{\otimes k}) only relates to the spectrum \eta of \rho, as proved in Lemma below. Thus, we use \text{SW}_{\rho}^k(\lambda) to denote the weak Schur sampling probability \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) where \lambda is the eigenvalue of the density matrix \rho.

ImportantLemma

Defined \text{dim}(\lambda) as the number of standard Young tableaus of shape \lambda \vdash k and alphabet [k]. Then \text{SW}_{\rho}^k(\lambda)= \text{dim}(\lambda) \cdot s_\lambda (\eta_1,\cdots,\eta_d) with \eta the spectrum of \rho. Specifically, we have \text{SW}_{d^{-1}\mathbb{I}}^k(\lambda) = {(\text{dim} (\lambda))^2}{(k!)^{-1}} {d^{\uparrow \lambda}}({d^k})^{-1}, where denots d^{\uparrow \lambda}: = \prod_{(i,j) \in [\lambda]} (d + j - i) with i,j labeling the position of all the lattices in Young tableaus of shape \lambda \vdash n,

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. \begin{align} \label{eq:Schur_prob} \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) = (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \text{tr}( \text{SWAP}_\pi \rho^{\otimes k}). \end{align} If \pi has l cycles with cycle length \kappa_1\cdots\kappa_l and \rho has eigenvalues \eta_1,\cdots,\eta_{d}, we noted that \begin{align} \text{tr}( \text{SWAP}_\pi \rho^{\otimes k}) = \text{tr}(\rho^{\kappa_1})\times \cdots\times\text{tr}(\rho^{\kappa_l}) = M_{\kappa}(\eta). \end{align} Plug into Eq.~(eq:Schur_prob) gives \begin{align} \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) &= (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) M_{\kappa}(\eta)\\ &=(\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \sum_{\omega \vdash k}\chi_{\omega}(\pi)s_{\omega}(\eta)\\ &=(\text{dim}\lambda) \cdot s_{\lambda}(\eta). \end{align} Here in the second equality, we use Lemma. In the third equality, we use the orthorgonal equation of group characters |G|^{-1} \sum_{g \in G} \chi_{p}^*(g)\chi_{q}(g) = \delta_{pq}. ◻
